authors: Chitchumnong, P.; Hatairatana, A.; Khangphukhieo, W.
title: Physical Climate Risk Stress Test: An Evidence-based Approach
venue: CRC Working Papers, Credit Research Centre, University of Edinburgh
question: What was the impact of the 2011 Thai flood on a bank's mortgage default, and how can it feed a physical climate stress test?
data: Proprietary Thai bank mortgage portfolio 2009-2013; Royal Irrigation Department runoff at Nakhon Sawan since 1979
identification: Vintage (age-period-cohort) default model: benchmark plus macro variables (lower bound); flood-affected vs unaffected borrower lifecycles (upper bound); extreme value analysis for scenario probability
main_finding: Modest mortgage default impact, dampened by debt relief and rapid recovery; flood-affected borrowers riskier; auto-loan defaults spiked; 2011 runoff about 1-in-50-year event
how_my_project_differs: Collateral-level satellite exposure; LGD and IFRS 9 staging rather than default rates only; relief modelled as treatment; formal reverse stress test; multi-bank or public-data design

authors: Caloia, F.; Jansen, D.-J.
title: Flood risk and financial stability: Evidence from a stress test for the Netherlands
venue: De Nederlandsche Bank (paper dated 2 Nov 2021; series number not confirmed)
question: When would floods start impairing financial stability?
data: Geocoded real-estate exposures of ten Dutch banks (>95% of sector assets), loan-level and supervisory data, official flood maps at 4-digit postcode level
identification: Top-down stress test with PD module (interest-rate, business, collateral-repricing risk) and LGD module driven by collateral damage; escalating scenarios described as in essence a reverse stress test
main_finding: 110-132 bp extra CET1 depletion for floods in unprotected areas; well over 700 bp for extreme inundation in the protected west; residential damage drives LGD and RWA
how_my_project_differs: Emerging market with thin insurance and debt relief; observed satellite inundation rather than hazard maps; ECL and staging; formal inversion for breaching severity

authors: European Central Bank
title: 2022 climate risk stress test
question: How capable are euro area significant institutions of climate stress testing and how exposed are they?
data: Bank submissions (41 banks gave projections); NUTS3 flood-risk map from JRC and Four Twenty Seven data
identification: Constrained bottom-up supervisory stress test; flood and drought-heat scenarios; short- and 30-year transition scenarios
main_finding: About EUR 70bn losses, acknowledged as an understatement; credit parameters fairly insensitive to climate shocks; flood losses concentrated in high and medium risk areas; no direct capital implications
how_my_project_differs: Tests empirically whether provisions and parameters respond to observed floods; finer than NUTS3; emerging-market setting

authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: Pilot Climate Scenario Analysis Exercise: Summary of Participants' Risk-Management Practices and Estimates
question: How do large US banks translate physical and transition scenarios into credit risk parameters?
data: Six large banks' submissions; Northeast hurricane shocks (100- and 200-year return period losses, 2050) plus idiosyncratic shocks
identification: Supervisory scenario analysis; static balance sheet; no-insurance assumption; existing PD/LGD models with damage passed through LTV and DSCR
main_finding: Banks mostly reused existing models; data gaps on building characteristics and insurance; insurance assumptions pivotal; heterogeneous PD impacts
how_my_project_differs: Where insurance is thin, relief replaces insurance as the key assumption; estimated rather than assumed damage-to-PD/LGD links

authors: Bank of England
title: Results of the 2021 Climate Biennial Exploratory Scenario (CBES)
verified: verified 2026-11-02 via BoE web page (automated summary)
question: How resilient are large UK banks and insurers to three 30-year climate scenarios?
data: Participant submissions from UK banks, building societies and insurers
identification: Exploratory bottom-up scenario exercise (Early Action, Late Action, No Additional Action)
main_finding: Impairment rates just over 50% above normal under No Additional Action; 45% of mortgage impairments in 10% of 4-digit postcode areas; not used to set capital requirements
how_my_project_differs: Collateral-level rather than postcode concentration; empirical validation with observed floods; emerging market

authors: Alogoskoufis, S.; Dunz, N.; Emambakhsh, T.; Hennig, T.; Kaijser, M.; et al.
title: ECB's economy-wide climate stress test
question: How would firms and euro area banks be affected by climate risk under alternative policy paths over 30 years?
data: Climate and financial data on millions of firms and about 1,600 euro area banks
identification: Top-down economy-wide stress test with climate-specific firm and bank models
main_finding: Physical risk dominates long-run losses without transition policy, rises non-linearly and concentrates in vulnerable regions and banks
how_my_project_differs: Event-based, collateral-level micro evidence instead of top-down long-horizon projections

authors: Acharya, V.V.; Berner, R.; Engle, R.; Jung, H.; Stroebel, J.; Zeng, X.; Zhao, Y.
title: Climate Stress Testing
verified: verified 2026-11-02 via Crossref; NBER WP 31097 read
question: How should climate stress tests be designed and where is research needed?
data: Review of regulatory scenarios and literature
identification: Review article
main_finding: Calls for work on short-run credit channels given loan maturities, bank lending responses, adequacy of risk pricing and expectation formation; proposes market-based tests as complements
how_my_project_differs: Supplies short-run credit-channel evidence from realised floods in an emerging market

authors: Jung, H.; Engle, R.; Berner, R.
title: CRISK: Measuring the Climate Risk Exposure of the Financial System
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Reports 977 (2021, revised 2025)
question: Are banks sufficiently capitalised to absorb losses under heightened climate transition risk?
data: Bank stock returns; climate transition risk factors (e.g. stranded asset factor); FR Y-14Q loan data for validation
identification: Market-based expected capital shortfall using dynamic climate betas; stress at 1st percentile of 6-month factor returns
main_finding: Climate betas rose from 2019 and peaked in 2020; loan-portfolio betas align with market-based betas
how_my_project_differs: Physical, collateral-level, bottom-up credit approach; a market-based variant could serve a public-data Plan B

authors: Dhima, J.; Iravani, M.A.; Itam, E.; Boidot, T.
title: Integration of physical climate risks into banks' credit risk and capital assessment: a case study on the impact of flooding on real estate portfolios
question: How can banks integrate river-flood damage into PD, LGD and internal capital?
data: Case study of real estate portfolios (details not read)
identification: Extended Merton (1974) structural model with flood damage to collateral
main_finding: Flooding affects PD, LGD and capital, but not systematically when damage is below expected return on immovable assets; material for already-vulnerable firms
how_my_project_differs: Empirical estimation with observed floods and Thai collateral; adds IFRS 9 staging and reverse stress test

authors: Lepore, C.; Mok, J.
title: Beyond the Dikes: Flood Scenarios for Financial Stability Risk Analysis
question: How do different flood scenarios affect Dutch bank capital?
data: Flood scenarios by region, type, climate, return period and adaptation (details not read)
identification: Damage-calibrated macro-financial scenarios in a bank stress test
main_finding: Capital impact varies greatly by scenario; climate change amplifies, defences mitigate; non-linear damage-capital relationship
how_my_project_differs: Emerging market; collateral-level exposure; inversion to find breaching severity

authors: Shala, I.; Schumacher, B.
title: The impact of natural disasters on banks' impairment flow - Evidence from Germany
verified: verified 2026-11-02 via Crossref and Bundesbank DP PDF
question: How did regionally focused German banks' loan loss provisioning respond to the 2013 flood?
data: German savings and cooperative bank data; county disaster information
identification: Difference-in-differences; treatment by region of primary operations; neighbouring-county controls
main_finding: Higher but ephemeral impairment flow, driven by corporate (agriculture, manufacturing) and some mortgage loans; authors conclude expected-loss provisioning was insufficient
how_my_project_differs: Loan-level collateral exposure and IFRS 9 staging; thin-insurance emerging market with debt relief

authors: Dal Maso, L.; Kanagaretnam, K.; Lobo, G.J.; Mazzi, F.
title: Does Disaster Risk Relate to Banks' Loan Loss Provisions?
question: Do banks' loan loss provisions reflect local disaster risk?
data: More than 445,000 US bank-quarter observations; FEMA major-disaster declarations over 15 years
identification: Panel regressions with disaster-risk measure; difference-in-differences and matched samples
main_finding: Banks in higher disaster-risk counties recognise larger loan loss provisions
how_my_project_differs: Collateral-level satellite hazard and IFRS 9 ECL rather than county declarations and US provisioning

authors: Correa, R.; He, A.; Herpfer, C.; Lel, U.
title: The Rising Tide Lifts Some Interest Rates: Climate Change, Natural Disasters, and Loan Pricing
question: Do banks update loan pricing after climate-related disasters?
data: Syndicated loans in primary and secondary markets (details not read)
identification: Borrowers at risk of but not hit by disasters vs others; climate vs non-climate disasters
main_finding: Spreads spike for at-risk borrowers after climate disasters, not after non-climate ones; short-lived and salience-driven
how_my_project_differs: Provisioning and collateral valuation rather than spreads; emerging-market bank loans

authors: Grundke, P.; Pliszka, K.
title: A macroeconomic reverse stress test
venue: Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting 50(4):1093-1130
question: How to find the most probable scenarios that make a bank fail?
data: Empirical calibration for a maturity-transforming bank (details not read)
identification: Inversion of a credit and interest-rate risk model over macro factors; PCA; copulas; extreme value theory
main_finding: Inversion and scenario probabilities in one model are feasible, but results carry considerable model and estimation risk
how_my_project_differs: Applies inversion to a physical hazard variable (flood severity) rather than macro factors

authors: Glasserman, P.; Kang, C.; Kang, W.
title: Stress scenario selection by empirical likelihood
question: How to select the most likely scenarios leading to losses above a threshold?
data: Market factor and portfolio loss distributions
identification: Non-parametric empirical likelihood for conditional mean of factors given large losses; tail-dependent scaling
main_finding: Provides justified confidence regions for most likely loss scenarios under elliptical distributions
how_my_project_differs: Hazard-driven credit loss rather than market factors

authors: Luangaram, P.; Sethapramote, Y.; Thampanishvong, K.; Uddin, G.S.
title: Climate Risk and Financial Stability: A Systemic Risk Perspective from Thailand
verified: verified 2026-11-02 via PIER PDF and RePEc
question: How do transition and physical risks affect systemic risk of Thai banks?
data: SET stock data; brown-minus-green factor; SPEI index
identification: Bank-level CoVaR; panel regressions with Fama-French factors and macro controls
main_finding: Transition risk (BMG) significantly raises systemic risk; physical risk, especially floods, challenges bank portfolios
how_my_project_differs: Loan- and collateral-level credit channel rather than market-based systemic risk with an index hazard

authors: Dolk, M.; Dunz, N.; Lesage, F.; Nie, O.; Pollitt, H.

venue: World Bank Blogs, All About Finance

how_my_project_differs: Collateral-level rather than district-level exposure; PD/LGD/ECL estimation; reverse stress test
